title: Mindfulness of death
hookLine: the Buddha asks his monks how they recall death, and the answers shrink from a day to a single breath

cards: A hall built of brick, and a group of monks seated before their teacher. The Buddha asks them a direct question: do you practice mindfulness of death? Yes, says one, and explains how.

Yes, says another, and explains differently. As they go around the room, something odd happens. The span each one names gets shorter and shorter, from a whole day, to a meal, to a mouthful, to a single breath.
The Buddha listens to all of them, then tells them which ones have understood.

teach.b: First, the word. Maranasati is Pali: marana, death, and sati, mindfulness. In this discourse the Buddha says that when it is developed, it brings great fruit and leads toward the deathless.
Second, the long spans. The first monk thinks: if only I might live one more day and night, I could attend to the teaching and do much. Another says the same about a single day.

teach.h: A DAY, A MEAL: TOO SLOW.
teach.b: Another, as long as it takes to eat one meal. Another, while he chews and swallows a few mouthfuls of food. The Buddha's verdict is quiet but firm: they are living heedlessly.
Their mindfulness of death is too slow. Third, the short spans.
One monk says: just for the time it takes to chew and swallow one mouthful. Another: just for the time between breathing in and breathing out, or breathing out and breathing in.
These two, the Buddha says, are heedful, developing mindfulness of death keenly. Fourth, why the breath.
The point isn't fear. It's attention. A day feels long enough to put things off.

If you only count on this breath, the next unkind word, the next put-off apology, the next thing you meant to notice, is happening now or not at all. The Buddha tells the monks to train this way: we will live heedfully.
Some Buddhists today practice this recollection with a short phrase, some simply with the breath.

how: Some Buddhists practice maranasati, mindfulness of death, as a regular recollection: some repeat a short reflection that life is uncertain and death is certain, others simply attend to each breath as if it were the one they can count on.

o: a Buddhist funeral chant recited for those who have died
a fast that monks keep to prepare for their own deaths
mindfulness of death, kept as close as a single breath

games.q: the monks' answers — tap the pairs.

s: the Buddha praised the monk who recalled death for a whole day
a day was too slow; one mouthful and one breath were heedful.
maranasati joins the words for death and mindfulness
the point of the practice is to be afraid
the point is attention: living heedfully, now.

games.q: the Buddha asks how you recall death. which answer does he call heedful?
o: if only I might live one more day and night.
for as long as one meal.
between one breath and the next.
games.why: the long spans he calls heedless. one mouthful and one breath: those monks are living heedfully.

practice: Take one breath as if it were the only one you could count on, not dramatically, just fully: the cool at the nose, the rise of the chest, the long breath out.

Then the next, the same way, and if the mind jumps ahead to later today, come back to this breath. If the idea of a last breath feels heavy right now, drop it and simply attend to each breath as it comes.

wordCard.voice: Maranasati: Pali for mindfulness of death, practiced in the Buddha's teaching down to the span of a single breath. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali, written here in Devanagari: maraṇasati, mindfulness of death (also written maraṇassati).

carryVoice: Your line: this breath. Not fear, but attention, one breath at a time. Day seven hundred sixty-four, done.
